newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe's divisions on display for all to see.
newsitem.headline: Europe's divisions on display for all to see.

text.p: European Union leaders returned home on Wednesday from their two-day mid-year summit in Amsterdam with a watered-down treaty, a patched-up agreement on monetary union and Europe's divisions on display for all to see.
Small countries fought large ones. Reluctant integrationists dug in their heels against federalists. Economic "dirigists" clashed with the disciples of budgetary rigour.
The Franco-German alliance, the bloc's once-powerful motor, was hardly to be seen.

Spain even put on a show of the kind of self-serving brinkmanship the treaty was supposed to address, holding up agreement of the new treaty for hours into the night to make sure it got a last-minute concession.

The result was a treaty that leaders themselves said failed to meet the modest goals EU leaders had set, and an agreement on economic and monetary union (EMU) that analysts said simply papered over problems that will erupt again.
"We should be able to round off EMU and move to enlargement," Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said in less than dynamic terms.

Enlargement into formerly Communist eastern Europe -- the historic move the new treaty was supposed to prepare for -- will not be damaged by the failure to make institutional reforms, officials insisted.
These would include a measure allowing majority voting instead of the current unanimous system.
But the officials added that nothing had been done to help institutional reforms along.
In fact, one decision was seen by eastern European applicants to have thrown up a hurdle to their bloc membership.

Seeking to avoid a drag-out fight between the bloc's small and large countries over power-sharing, the leaders effectively deferred decisions on institutional reform for another constitutional review.

This would be triggered once the bloc's numbers reach 20, five more than it currently has. With 11 countries having been promised membership, only the most obvious first-wave entrants such as Hungary are undisturbed by this development.
Although few would say so publicly, the Amsterdam summit also raised questions about the EU's ability and desire to meet lofty goals of political integration, including a common foreign policy.

Officials said the leaders simply did not have the stomach for the kind of fight that would be necessary. Germany even stepped out of character and blocked some moves towards integration it would normally have been expected to trumpet.

But officials also said that many leaders were keen to push divisions off the table, believing that the single currency to be launched in January 1999 would provide the unifying framework needed to put the bloc back on track.

In a makeshift deal on Monday, the bloc met some of France's demands that employment and political control of EMU get more attention in order to secure agreement on the stability pact, the framework for budgetary discipline after EMU is launched.

The deal was widely viewed as a fudge, but one that underlined the absolute commitment of the mainstream EU countries to go ahead with the project -- albeit probably with a weak euro in a broad range of countries.

The underlying dispute between France and Germany over institutional control of monetary union, however, presaged serious problems both in the run-up to the launch and, perhaps more importantly, afterwards.

As for the Franco-German alliance, Bonn's domestic problems and the new political landscape in Paris rendered it mostly impotent. Nearly all its proposals -- for example the incorporation into the EU of the Western European Union defence grouping -- were blocked or diluted.
French Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine admitted that it was getting harder for the two countries to keep in step.
"Germany is having problems it did not have before. France is evolving, it has its problems and its social demands, its new political situation," he said on French radio.
Britain, Denmark, and Ireland, in the meantime, all left the summit with opt-outs in their pockets while a number of plans for further integration were simply shelved.
The treaty, in response, accepted for the first time that some countries did not want to integrate as fast as others.
At the summit itself, French President Jacques Chirac was asked why there were so many difficulties. His reply was that with 15 countries it is hard to find accord.
The Amsterdam summit was supposed to prepare the way for an EU with anything from 25 to 30 countries.
